edits.title: Docker Namespace Types
bullets: PID namespace isolates process IDs, giving each container its own independent process numbering.
UTS namespace provides a separate hostname and domain name for each container.
MNT namespace gives each container its own mount point hierarchy.
IPC namespace isolates inter‑process communication resources such as shared memory and semaphores.
NET namespace supplies each container with its own network stack, interfaces, and routing tables.
USER namespace maps container user IDs to host IDs, allowing non‑root processes inside containers.
addresses_questions: What are the main types of namespaces Docker uses?
What is a Linux namespace and why does Docker use them?

edits.title: Concrete cgroup hierarchy and resource‑limit example
bullets: Create a parent cgroup “/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/parent” and set memory.limit_in_bytes to 200 MB.
Create a child cgroup “/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/parent/child” and set memory.limit_in_bytes to 100 MB.
Add a process ID to the child cgroup by writing the PID to child/tasks; the process inherits the 100 MB limit.
A process started in the child cgroup cannot exceed 100 MB, while a sibling in the parent cgroup can use up to 200 MB.
Child cgroups inherit all limits from their ancestors; tighter limits in a child override the parent’s higher limits.

edits.title: Concrete Automation to Eliminate Manual Bottlenecks
bullets: Use Infrastructure‑as‑Code tools (Terraform, CloudFormation) to provision environments automatically.
Run database migrations with scripts (Flyway, Liquibase) triggered by the pipeline.
Scan container images for vulnerabilities during the build step.
Retrieve secrets from a vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) instead of manual entry.
Define automated rollback steps that redeploy the previous successful image on failure.

edits.title: Historical Goals & Incentives of Development vs. Operations
bullets: Developers were measured on speed of feature delivery, sprint velocity, and number of releases per period.
Operations were measured on system stability, uptime, SLA compliance, and cost efficiency of infrastructure.
Developers prioritized rapid changes to meet market demand, often pushing code without full testing.
Operations prioritized reliability and risk mitigation, preferring fewer, well‑tested changes.
These differing metrics created tension: fast releases threatened stability, while strict stability slowed feature rollout.
addresses_questions: Why do development and operations teams historically have conflicting goals?
